Authors: Rinaldi S.M.; Peerenboom J.P.; Kelly T.K.
Title: Identifying Understanding and Analyzing Critical Infrastructure Interdependencies
Abstract: The notion that our nation's critical infrastructures are highly interconnected and mutually dependent in complex ways, both physically and through a host of information and communications technologies (so-called "cyberbased systems"), is more than an abstract, theoretical concept. As shown by the 1998 failure of the Galaxy 4 telecommunications satellite, the prolonged power crisis in California, and many other recent infrastructure disruptions, what happens to one infrastructure can directly and indirectly affect other infrastructures, impact large geographic regions and send ripples throughout the national a global economy. This article presents a conceptual framework for addressing infrastructure interdependencies that could serve as the basis for further understanding and scholarship in this important area. We use this framework to explore the challenges and complexities of interdependency. We set the stage for this discussion by explicitly defining the terms infrastructure, infrastructure dependencies, and infrastructure interdependencies and introducing the fundamental concept of infrastructures as complex adaptive systems. We then focus on the interrelated factors and system conditions that collectively define the six dimensions. Finally, we discuss some of the research challenges involved in developing, applying, and validating modeling and simulation methodologies and tools for infrastructure interdependency analysis.

Authors: Bruneau M.; Chang S.E.; Eguchi R.T.; et al.
Title: A Framework to Quantitatively Assess and Enhance the Seismic Resilience of Communities
Abstract: This paper presents a conceptual framework to define seismic resilience of communities and quantitative measures of resilience that can be useful for a coordinated research effort focusing on enhancing this resilience. This framework relies on the complementary measures of resilience: “Reduced failure probabilities,” “Reduced consequences from failures,” and “Reduced time to recovery.” The framework also includes quantitative measures of the “ends” of robustness and rapidity, and the “means” of resourcefulness and redundancy, and integrates those measures into the four dimensions of community resilience—technical, organizational, social, and economic—all of which can be used to quantify measures of resilience for various types of physical and organizational systems. Systems diagrams then establish the tasks required to achieve these objectives. This framework can be useful in future research to determine the resiliency of different units of analysis and systems, and to develop resiliency targets and detailed analytical procedures to generate these values.

Authors: Fotouhi H.; Moryadee S.; Miller-Hooks E.
Title: Quantifying the resilience of an urban traffic-electric power coupled system
Abstract: A bi-level mixed-integer stochastic program quantifies resilience of a coupled traffic-power network using a two-layer representation, linking variables and logical constraints under hazard scenarios. A Minneapolis case study shows explicit infrastructure interdependencies materially affect transportation resilience estimates.
Why retained: Explicitly models coupled traffic and electric-power resilience with linking variables and stochastic optimization.

Authors: Wei W.; Wu D.; Wu Q.; Shafie-Khah M.; Catalao J.
Title: Interdependence between transportation system and power distribution system: a comprehensive review on models and applications
Source title: Journal of Modern Power Systems and Clean Energy
Abstract: Reviews power distribution and transportation models, user equilibrium, power flow, and explicit interdependence through EV charging stations, covering planning and operation and identifying prospective research directions.
Why retained: Reviews the mathematical building blocks of power–transportation interdependence, including traffic equilibrium and power flow.

Authors: Wu F.; Yang J.; Jiang H.; et al.
Title: Cascading failure in coupled networks of transportation and power grid
Source title: International Journal of Electrical Power & Energy Systems
Abstract: Models cascading failure in coupled transportation and power networks with large-scale EV charging loads. EV behavior and transportation states under failures are coupled to power-grid load-capacity failure propagation.
Why retained: Models EV-mediated cascading propagation between transportation and power networks.

Authors: Sadhu K.; Haghshenas K.; Rouhani M.; et al.
Title: Optimal joint operation of coupled transportation and power distribution urban networks
Abstract: Develops joint stochastic operational planning of transportation and power distribution networks under increasing EV penetration, combining transportation assignment and power-system operation to capture temporally varying interactions.
Why retained: Represents joint stochastic operation of transportation and power-distribution networks.

Authors: Oladigbolu et al.
Title: A review on transport and power systems planning-operation integrating electric vehicles, energy storage, and other distributed energy resources
Abstract: Decision-oriented review of coupled power-transportation systems integrating network-flow representations with planning, scheduling, resilience, EV, storage, mobile resources, deterministic, stochastic, robust and learning-optimization methods.
Why retained: Decision-oriented review connecting network models, resilience, EV flexibility, and implementable controls.

Authors: Lu Q.-C.; Wang S.; Xu P.-C.; et al.
Title: Modeling the dependency relationship of coupled power and transportation networks
Abstract: Proposes a supply-demand-based dependency model for coupled power and transportation networks that represents functional heterogeneity of fast charging stations and studies how charging price and redundancy affect dependency strength.
Why retained: Quantifies P–T dependency using supply–demand relations and heterogeneous fast-charging stations.

Authors: Yang M.; Chen Y.; Huang S.; Chen L.
Title: Recent advances in coordination and optimization of power-transportation systems: An overview
Abstract: Reviews basic power-transportation models, nonconvex optimization, pricing and coordination, uncertainty, pilot projects, planning, operation, resilience enhancement and market participation.
Why retained: Synthesizes current mathematical coordination, optimization, uncertainty, and resilience methods for P–T systems.

Authors: Wang S.; Lu Q.-C.; Liu L.; Xu P.-C.; Wang R.; Zhang L.
Title: Interdependency analysis of coupled power and transportation networks considering the charging decision preferences of EV drivers
Abstract: Uses a supply-demand-based interdependency model to study coupled power-transportation networks under disasters and shows EV-driver charging preferences and risk perceptions significantly change network interdependency.
Why retained: Shows that EV charging decisions can change measured P–T interdependency under disruption.

Authors: Ma C.; Yao C.; Hua H.; Lei S.
Title: Resilient pricing-driven coordination of coupled power and transportation networks: A learning-augmented mixed-integer reformulation approach
Abstract: Develops a bilevel resilient pricing framework coordinating power distribution restoration with dynamic traffic and energy assignment, using V2G flexibility and mixed-integer reformulation; case studies show improved restoration.
Why retained: Couples dynamic traffic-energy assignment, V2G, and distribution-system restoration in a resilience decision model.

Authors: Clark et al.
Title: The vulnerability of interdependent urban infrastructure systems to climate change: could Phoenix experience a Katrina of extreme heat?
Abstract: Applies resilience theory to interdependent water, power and transportation infrastructure under extreme heat in Phoenix, emphasizing amplified stressors and sensing, anticipating, adapting and learning.
Why retained: Connects extreme heat with interdependent urban infrastructure stress and resilience.

Authors: Visakh A.; Selvan M.P.
Title: Analysis and mitigation of the impact of electric vehicle charging on service disruption of distribution transformers
Abstract: Models EV charging impacts on distribution-transformer apparent power, top-oil and hottest-spot temperature, showing sustained overload can cause thermal service disruption and evaluating controlled charging mitigation.
Why retained: Links EV charging to transformer thermal state, service disruption, and controlled-charging mitigation.

Authors: Wang J.; Wang H.; Wang C.
Title: Optimal Charging Pile Configuration and Charging Scheduling for Electric Bus Routes Considering the Impact of Ambient Temperature on Charging Power
Abstract: Models ambient-temperature effects on battery charging performance and jointly optimizes depot charging-pile configuration and bus charging schedules using mixed-integer nonlinear programming and a real depot case.
Why retained: Directly couples ambient temperature, battery charging performance, and electric-bus depot scheduling.

Authors: Hendriks J.N.; Sturmberg B.C.P.
Title: An integrated model of electric bus energy consumption and optimised depot charging
Abstract: Integrates data-driven electric-bus energy consumption with depot charging optimization; route topology, temperature and traffic congestion affect energy use, charging infrastructure, battery design and grid loading.
Why retained: Links temperature and traffic to electric-bus energy states, depot charging, and grid loading.

Authors: Zakaria A.; Duan C.; Djokic S.Z.
Title: Hosting capacity of distribution networks for controlled and uncontrolled residential EV charging with static and dynamic thermal ratings of network components
Abstract: Combines actual EV charging data, Monte Carlo demand profiles, weather data, and static/dynamic thermal ratings of distribution components to quantify EV hosting capacity under controlled and uncontrolled charging.
Why retained: Uses weather-dependent dynamic thermal ratings to quantify EV hosting limits and charging control.

Authors: Parker N.C.; Kuby M.; Liu J.; Stechel E.B.
Title: Extreme heat effects on electric vehicle energy consumption and driving range
Abstract: Uses 345,622 real BEV trips from Phoenix to quantify temperature-dependent energy consumption and range. At 46–50 C energy use rises about 25–28% and future EV charging demand increases on the hottest days.
Why retained: Quantifies how extreme heat changes EV energy use, driving range, and future grid charging demand.

Authors: Gupta A.K.; Verma K.
Title: Dynamic thermal impact of heatwaves on resilience of power system considering transmission line and generators capacities
Abstract: Dynamically couples IEEE 738 line ampacity using ambient temperature, wind and solar radiation with temperature-dependent generator derating; stochastic heatwave scenarios and sequential Monte Carlo assess resilience.
Why retained: Dynamically maps heatwave weather variables to thermal limits and power-system resilience.

Authors: Martinez et al.
Title: Grid Resilience Enhancement Under Extreme Heat Wave Events
Abstract: Models extreme-heat distribution-grid stress from increased demand and reduced line capacity, using probabilistic simulation and resilience-oriented dispatch of distributed resources and storage.
Why retained: Models distribution-grid resilience under extreme heat with reduced capacity and elevated demand.

Authors: Krama A.; Kamal N.; Sezer N.; Bayhan S.
Title: Impact of extreme climatic conditions on fast EV charger performance: field experimental insights from Qatar
Abstract: Field measurements of a 50 kW air-cooled DC fast charger across 15–55 C show severe thermal derating; rectifier temperature explains over 96% of offered-power variation and peak heat nearly doubles charging duration.
Why retained: Provides field evidence of temperature-driven fast-charger thermal derating and longer charging time.

Authors: Kong L.; Zhang H.; Xie D.; Dai N.-Y.
Title: Leveraging Electric Vehicles to Enhance Resilience of Interconnected Power-Transportation System Under Natural Hazards
Abstract: Proposes a two-stage scenario-based scheduling framework in which EVs are preallocated and redispatched through the transportation network as mobile energy resources to restore damaged interconnected power-transportation systems under natural hazards.
Why retained: Uses EV mobility and V2G as cross-system restoration resources under natural hazards.

Authors: Lian X.; Qiu L.; Song C.; Liu L.; Xu Z.
Title: Enhancing resilience of power-transportation coupled networks to typhoons: A tri-stage integration strategy of multi-resources
Abstract: Proposes a tri-stage resilience method for coupled power-transportation networks combining pre-event hardening, failure response, and restoration using repair crews and mobile storage under typhoon hazards.
Why retained: Provides a staged defend–respond–restore architecture for coupled P–T resilience.

Authors: Bai Y.; Cao D.; Hu W.; Huang Q.; Chen Z.
Title: Resilience Enhancement Strategy for Distribution Networks Under Extreme Heat Weather Using Collaborative Electric Vehicle Charging Stations
Abstract: Under extreme heat, coordinates EV charging stations using multi-agent deep reinforcement learning and V2G to support critical distribution nodes and minimize load shedding.
Why retained: Tests coordinated EV charging/V2G as an operational resilience action during extreme heat.
